## The Jordan Canonical Form

Let $\mathsf T$ be a linear operator on a finite-dimensional vector space $\mathsf V$ over $F$, and assume its characteristic polynomial splits into linear factors over $F$. A Jordan canonical basis $\beta$ puts its matrix into block-diagonal form:

$$
[\mathsf{T}]_\beta = \begin{pmatrix}
A_1 & O & \dots & O \\
O & A_2 & \dots & O \\
\vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\
O & O & \dots & A_k
\end{pmatrix},
$$

where each $O$ is a zero matrix, and each $A_i$ is a square matrix of the form $(\lambda)$ or
$$
\begin{pmatrix}
\lambda & 1 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 \\
0 & \lambda & 1 & \dots & 0 & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & \lambda & 1 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & \lambda
\end{pmatrix}
$$

for some eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $\mathsf{T}$. Such a matrix $A_i$ is called a **Jordan block** corresponding to $\lambda$, and the matrix $[\mathsf{T}]_\beta$ is called a **Jordan canonical form** of $\mathsf{T}$. We also say that the ordered basis $\beta$ is a **Jordan canonical basis** for $\mathsf{T}$. Observe that each Jordan block $A_i$ is “almost” a diagonal matrix—in fact, $[\mathsf{T}]_\beta$ is a diagonal matrix if and only if each $A_i$ is of the form $(\lambda)$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Generalized Eigenvector

Let $\mathsf{T}$ be a linear operator on a vector space $\mathsf{V}$, and let $\lambda$ be a scalar. A nonzero vector $x$ in $\mathsf{V}$ is called a **generalized eigenvector of $\mathsf{T}$ corresponding to $\lambda$** if
$$
(\mathsf{T} - \lambda\mathsf{I})^p(x) = 0
$$
for some positive integer $p$.

Notice that if $x$ is a generalized eigenvector of $\mathsf{T}$ corresponding to $\lambda$, and $p$ is the smallest positive integer for which $(\mathsf{T} - \lambda\mathsf{I})^p(x) = 0$, then $(\mathsf{T} - \lambda\mathsf{I})^{p-1}(x)$ is an eigenvector of $\mathsf{T}$ corresponding to $\lambda$. Therefore $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $\mathsf{T}$.

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Generalized Eigenspace

Let $\mathsf{T}$ be a linear operator on a vector space $\mathsf{V}$, and let $\lambda$ be an eigenvalue of $\mathsf{T}$. The **generalized eigenspace of $\mathsf{T}$ corresponding to** $\lambda$, denoted $\mathsf{K}_\lambda$, is the subset of $\mathsf{V}$ defined by
$$
\mathsf{K}_\lambda = \{x \in \mathsf{V} : (\mathsf{T} - \lambda\mathsf{I})^p(x) = 0 \text{ for some positive integer } p\}.
$$

Note that $\mathsf{K}_\lambda$ consists of the zero vector and all generalized eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda$.

:::

## Generalized Eigenspace Properties

::: {#thm-la-7-generalized-1}

Let $\mathsf{T}$ be a linear operator on a vector space $\mathsf{V}$, and let $\lambda$ be an eigenvalue of $\mathsf{T}$. Then:

- $\mathsf{K}_\lambda$ is a $\mathsf{T}$-invariant subspace of $\mathsf{V}$ containing $\mathsf{E}_\lambda$.

- For any scalar $\mu \neq \lambda$, the restriction of $\mathsf{T} - \mu\mathsf{I}$ to $\mathsf{K}_\lambda$ is one-to-one.

:::

::: {#thm-la-7-generalized-2}

Let $\mathsf{T}$ be a linear operator on a finite-dimensional vector space $\mathsf{V}$ such that the characteristic polynomial of $\mathsf{T}$ splits. Suppose that $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $\mathsf{T}$ with multiplicity $m$. Then:

- $\dim(\mathsf{K}_\lambda) \le m$.

- $\mathsf{K}_\lambda = \mathsf{N}((\mathsf{T} - \lambda\mathsf{I})^m)$.

:::

::: {#thm-la-7-generalized-3}

Let $\mathsf{T}$ be a linear operator on a finite-dimensional vector space $\mathsf{V}$ such that the characteristic polynomial of $\mathsf{T}$ splits, and let $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \dots, \lambda_k$ be the distinct eigenvalues of $\mathsf{T}$. Then, for every $x \in \mathsf{V}$, there exist vectors $v_i \in \mathsf{K}_{\lambda_i}$, $1 \le i \le k$, such that
$$
x = v_1 + v_2 + \dots + v_k.
$$

:::

::: {#thm-la-7-generalized-4}

Let $\mathsf{T}$ be a linear operator on a finite-dimensional vector space $\mathsf{V}$ such that the characteristic polynomial of $\mathsf{T}$ splits, and let $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \dots, \lambda_k$ be the distinct eigenvalues of $\mathsf{T}$ with corresponding multiplicities $m_1, m_2, \dots, m_k$. For $1 \le i \le k$, let $\beta_i$ be an ordered basis for $\mathsf{K}_{\lambda_i}$. Then the following statements are true.

- $\beta_i \cap \beta_j = \varnothing$ for $i \neq j$.

- $\beta = \beta_1 \cup \beta_2 \cup \dots \cup \beta_k$ is an ordered basis for $\mathsf{V}$.

- $\dim(\mathsf{K}_{\lambda_i}) = m_i$ for all $i$.

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Cycles of Generalized Eigenvectors

Let $\mathsf{T}$ be a linear operator on a vector space $\mathsf{V}$, and let $x$ be a generalized eigenvector of $\mathsf{T}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda$. Suppose that $p$ is the smallest positive integer for which $(\mathsf{T} - \lambda\mathsf{I})^p(x) = 0$. Then the ordered set
$$
\{(\mathsf{T} - \lambda\mathsf{I})^{p-1}(x), (\mathsf{T} - \lambda\mathsf{I})^{p-2}(x), \dots, (\mathsf{T} - \lambda\mathsf{I})(x), x\}
$$
is called a **cycle of generalized eigenvectors** of $\mathsf{T}$ corresponding to $\lambda$. The vectors $(\mathsf{T} - \lambda\mathsf{I})^{p-1}(x)$ and $x$ are called the **initial vector** and the **end vector** of the cycle, respectively. We say that the **length** of the cycle is $p$.

:::

::: {#thm-la-7-1}

Let $\mathsf{T}$ be a linear operator on a finite-dimensional vector space $\mathsf{V}$ whose characteristic polynomial splits, and suppose that $\beta$ is a basis for $\mathsf{V}$ such that $\beta$ is a disjoint union of cycles of generalized eigenvectors of $\mathsf{T}$. Then the following statements are true.
(a) For each cycle $\gamma$ of generalized eigenvectors contained in $\beta$, $\mathsf{W} = \operatorname{span}(\gamma)$ is $\mathsf{T}$-invariant, and $[\mathsf{T}_{\mathsf{W}}]_\gamma$ is a Jordan block.
(b) $\beta$ is a Jordan canonical basis for $\mathsf{V}$.

:::

::: {#thm-la-7-2}

Let $\mathsf{T}$ be a linear operator on a vector space $\mathsf{V}$, and let $\lambda$ be an eigenvalue of $\mathsf{T}$. Suppose that $\gamma_1, \gamma_2, \dots, \gamma_q$ are cycles of generalized eigenvectors of $\mathsf{T}$ corresponding to $\lambda$ such that the initial vectors of the $\gamma_i$'s are distinct and form a linearly independent set. Then the $\gamma_i$'s are disjoint, and their union $\gamma = \bigcup_{i=1}^q \gamma_i$ is linearly independent.

:::

::: {#thm-la-7-existence name="Existence and Uniqueness of Jordan Form"}

If the characteristic polynomial of a linear operator on a finite-dimensional vector space splits over the base field, then a Jordan canonical basis exists. Its Jordan blocks are unique up to their order.

In particular, every complex square matrix is similar to a Jordan matrix. For an eigenvalue $\lambda$, the number of Jordan blocks equals the dimension of its eigenspace, and the sum of their sizes equals its algebraic multiplicity.

:::

Reference: [MIT 18.700: Jordan Normal Form Notes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-034-honors-differential-equations-spring-2004/51c72a6989c6a79228158a69f7750c5a_normal.pdf).
